lines.text: The Fed may hike. So why did mortgage rates fall?
lines.say: The Fed may hike. So why did mortgage rates fall?

lines.text: Freddie Mac says the average 30-year mortgage rate fell for a fourth straight week, to 7.11%.
lines.say: Freddie Mac says the average thirty-year mortgage rate fell for a fourth straight week, to seven point one one percent.

lines.text: That same week, inflation came in hot, and a Fed governor floated a half-point rate hike.
lines.say: That same week, inflation came in hot, and a Fed governor floated a half-point rate hike.

lines.text: Rates heading up, mortgages heading down. It sounds backwards, but it's one of the most useful things to understand about money.
lines.say: Rates heading up, mortgages heading down. It sounds backwards, but it's one of the most useful things to understand about money.

lines.text: So today: the week inflation ran hot, why mortgages fell anyway, the dollar's big week, and what it all means for you.
lines.say: So today: the week inflation ran hot, why mortgages fell anyway, the dollar's big week, and what it all means for you.

lines.text: Because the Fed's next decision lands on December 9th, and it reaches your card, your savings and your paycheck.
lines.say: Because the Fed's next decision lands on December ninth, and it reaches your card, your savings and your paycheck.

lines.text: Chapter 1: A hot inflation week.
lines.say: Chapter one: a hot inflation week.

lines.text: It started Tuesday morning, with the government's October inflation report.
lines.say: It started Tuesday morning, with the government's October inflation report.

lines.text: Prices rose 0.4% in a single month. Economists had expected 0.3%.
lines.say: Prices rose zero point four percent in a single month. Economists had expected zero point three.

lines.text: A tenth of a point sounds tiny, but the Fed watches these tenths very closely.
lines.say: A tenth of a point sounds tiny, but the Fed watches these tenths very closely.

lines.text: Core prices, which leave out food and energy because they jump around, rose 0.3%. Forecasters expected 0.2%.
lines.say: Core prices, which leave out food and energy because they jump around, rose zero point three percent. Forecasters expected zero point two.

lines.text: Groceries were up 0.4% and gasoline 1% in that one month.
lines.say: Groceries were up zero point four percent and gasoline one percent in that one month.

lines.text: Here's the strange part. This report had no yearly inflation number at all.
lines.say: Here's the strange part. This report had no yearly inflation number at all.

lines.text: The 2025 government shutdown stopped the BLS from collecting prices in October 2025, so there was nothing to compare against.
lines.say: The twenty twenty-five government shutdown stopped the B L S from collecting prices in October twenty twenty-five, so there was nothing to compare against.

lines.text: The last yearly number we have is September's: prices up 3.7% from a year earlier.
lines.say: The last yearly number we have is September's: prices up three point seven percent from a year earlier.

lines.text: For scale, 0.4% a month, kept up for a full year, works out to about 4.9%. That's our math, and it's a pace, not a forecast.
lines.say: For scale, zero point four percent a month, kept up for a full year, works out to about four point nine percent. That's our math, and it's a pace, not a forecast.

lines.text: That same day, Fed Governor Christopher Waller gave a speech in London, and he was blunt about December.
lines.say: That same day, Fed Governor Christopher Waller gave a speech in London, and he was blunt about December.

lines.text: He said: "Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take."
lines.say: He said: hiking only twenty-five basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.

scene.text: Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.

lines.text: His starting point is a quarter-point hike. But if core prices kept rising about 0.3% a month, he said a half point should be considered.
lines.say: His starting point is a quarter-point hike. But if core prices kept rising about zero point three percent a month, he said a half point should be considered.

lines.text: Hours later, October's core number came in at 0.3%, right at the line he drew.
lines.say: Hours later, October's core number came in at zero point three percent, right at the line he drew.

lines.text: Bond traders reacted fast. The 10-year Treasury yield touched about 5% that day.
lines.say: Bond traders reacted fast. The ten-year Treasury yield touched about five percent that day.

lines.text: That matters because the 10-year is the benchmark lenders lean on for mortgages and car loans.
lines.say: That matters because the ten-year is the benchmark lenders lean on for mortgages and car loans.

lines.text: It's not a record, though. On October 7th it hit about 5.36%, its highest since 2002.
lines.say: It's not a record, though. On October seventh it hit about five point three six percent, its highest since two thousand two.

lines.text: Add it up: hot prices, a Fed governor talking about bigger hikes, and bond yields near 5%. That's a heavy week for rates.
lines.say: Add it up: hot prices, a Fed governor talking about bigger hikes, and bond yields near five percent. That's a heavy week for rates.

lines.text: Chapter 2: Why mortgages fell anyway.
lines.say: Chapter two: why mortgages fell anyway.

lines.text: So with all that going on, why did mortgage rates fall four weeks in a row?
lines.say: So with all that going on, why did mortgage rates fall four weeks in a row?

lines.text: First, they were falling from a high place. Freddie Mac's average hit 7.40% in early October, its highest in nearly 3 years.
lines.say: First, they were falling from a high place. Freddie Mac's average hit seven point four percent in early October, its highest in nearly three years.

lines.text: Then it slipped, week after week: 7.32, 7.24, 7.18, and now 7.11%, the lowest in seven weeks.
lines.say: Then it slipped, week after week: seven point three two, seven point two four, seven point one eight, and now seven point one one percent, the lowest in seven weeks.

lines.text: Freddie Mac's chief economist, Sam Khater, called it "a welcome development that gives borrowers greater flexibility."
lines.say: Freddie Mac's chief economist, Sam Khater, called it a welcome development that gives borrowers greater flexibility.

scene.text: Mortgage rates dropped to their lowest level in seven weeks, a welcome development that gives borrowers greater flexibility as they navigate the current housing market.

lines.text: Second, and this is the big one: the Fed doesn't set mortgage rates. It sets one short-term rate that banks charge each other overnight.
lines.say: Second, and this is the big one: the Fed doesn't set mortgage rates. It sets one short-term rate that banks charge each other overnight.

lines.text: Mortgages follow long-term bond yields, like the 10-year, and traders move those yields on what they expect the Fed to do, long before it acts.
lines.say: Mortgages follow long-term bond yields, like the ten-year, and traders move those yields on what they expect the Fed to do, long before it acts.

lines.text: A December hike was already largely priced in. So when yields eased from their October peak, mortgage rates eased with them.
lines.say: A December hike was already largely priced in. So when yields eased from their October peak, mortgage rates eased with them.

lines.text: We've seen this movie before, in reverse. In September 2024, the Fed cut its rate by half a point.
lines.say: We've seen this movie before, in reverse. In September twenty twenty-four, the Fed cut its rate by half a point.

lines.text: Mortgage rates were about 6.1% right after. By mid-January 2025, they were back above 7%.
lines.say: Mortgage rates were about six point one percent right after. By mid-January twenty twenty-five, they were back above seven percent.

lines.text: The Fed cut, and mortgages went up. It's the same lesson as this week, just flipped.
lines.say: The Fed cut, and mortgages went up. It's the same lesson as this week, just flipped.

lines.text: Here's the bigger picture: Freddie Mac's 30-year rate in mid-November of each of the last six years.
lines.say: Here's the bigger picture: Freddie Mac's thirty-year rate in mid-November of each of the last six years.

lines.text: In November 2021, the average was about 3.1%.
lines.say: In November twenty twenty-one, the average was about three point one percent.

lines.text: By November 2023, after the Fed's big hiking run, it was about 7.4%.
lines.say: By November twenty twenty-three, after the Fed's big hiking run, it was about seven point four percent.

lines.text: A year ago it had eased to about 6.2%.
lines.say: A year ago it had eased to about six point two percent.

lines.text: Now it's 7.11%, nearly a full point higher than a year ago, even after four weekly drops.
lines.say: Now it's seven point one one percent, nearly a full point higher than a year ago, even after four weekly drops.

lines.text: So the dip is real relief, but borrowing for a home still costs a lot more than it did last fall.
lines.say: So the dip is real relief, but borrowing for a home still costs a lot more than it did last fall.

lines.text: Chapter 3: The dollar's big week.
lines.say: Chapter three: the dollar's big week.

lines.text: The same rate bets that moved bond yields also pushed the dollar up.
lines.say: The same rate bets that moved bond yields also pushed the dollar up.

lines.text: On Thursday, the dollar index climbed above 103, its highest since April 2025.
lines.say: On Thursday, the dollar index climbed above one hundred three, its highest since April twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: That index measures the dollar against six major currencies, like the euro, the yen and the British pound.
lines.say: That index measures the dollar against six major currencies, like the euro, the yen and the British pound.

lines.text: Why is it rising? Money tends to flow toward higher interest rates, and traders are betting US rates go up again in December.
lines.say: Why is it rising? Money tends to flow toward higher interest rates, and traders are betting U S rates go up again in December.

lines.text: The flip side is Japan. This week the yen weakened to about 160 per dollar, a level that has made Tokyo nervous before.
lines.say: The flip side is Japan. This week the yen weakened to about one hundred sixty per dollar, a level that has made Tokyo nervous before.

lines.text: Japan's finance minister said the government will respond appropriately to currency moves.
lines.say: Japan's finance minister said the government will respond appropriately to currency moves.

lines.text: Here's a fact most people missed. In July, the yen sank to about 163 per dollar, its weakest since 1986.
lines.say: Here's a fact most people missed. In July, the yen sank to about one hundred sixty-three per dollar, its weakest since nineteen eighty-six.

lines.text: So the US and Japan stepped in together to buy yen, the first joint move like that since 1998.
lines.say: So the U S and Japan stepped in together to buy yen, the first joint move like that since nineteen ninety-eight.

lines.text: And now, a few months later, the yen is back near that 160 line.
lines.say: And now, a few months later, the yen is back near that one hundred sixty line.

lines.text: So who wins when the dollar is strong? Americans traveling abroad, and anyone buying imported goods, get more for each dollar.
lines.say: So who wins when the dollar is strong? Americans traveling abroad, and anyone buying imported goods, get more for each dollar.

lines.text: The losers are US companies that sell overseas. Their goods cost more abroad, and their foreign sales turn into fewer dollars.
lines.say: The losers are US companies that sell overseas. Their goods cost more abroad, and their foreign sales turn into fewer dollars.

lines.text: For Japan, it's the reverse. A weak yen makes imported food and fuel more expensive for Japanese families.
lines.say: For Japan, it's the reverse. A weak yen makes imported food and fuel more expensive for Japanese families.

lines.text: Chapter 4: Your loans, savings, paycheck.
lines.say: Chapter four: your loans, your savings, and your paycheck.

lines.text: Now the part that hits your wallet. The Fed's rate range today is 3.75% to 4%.
lines.say: Now the part that hits your wallet. The Fed's rate range today is three point seven five to four percent.

lines.text: A quarter-point hike in December would lift the top of that range to 4.25%. A half point would lift it to 4.5%.
lines.say: A quarter-point hike in December would lift the top of that range to four point two five percent. A half point would lift it to four point five.

lines.text: Credit cards feel it first. Most have variable rates, and Bankrate's average was about 19.7% in late October.
lines.say: Credit cards feel it first. Most have variable rates, and Bankrate's average was about nineteen point seven percent in late October.

lines.text: On a $5,000 balance, that's about $985 a year in interest, by our math.
lines.say: On a five thousand dollar balance, that's about nine hundred eighty-five dollars a year in interest, by our math.

lines.text: A quarter-point hike would add about $12.50 a year to that. A half point, about $25.
lines.say: A quarter-point hike would add about twelve dollars and fifty cents a year to that. A half point, about twenty-five dollars.

lines.text: So the hike itself is small money. The big cost is the nearly 20% already charged on any balance you carry.
lines.say: So the hike itself is small money. The big cost is the nearly twenty percent already charged on any balance you carry.

lines.text: Mortgages work differently. A fixed-rate loan you already have doesn't change at all.
lines.say: Mortgages work differently. A fixed-rate loan you already have doesn't change at all.

lines.text: For new loans, here's the gap. On a $400,000 loan, 7.11% is about $2,691 a month, versus about $2,460 a year ago at 6.24%.
lines.say: For new loans, here's the gap. On a four hundred thousand dollar loan, seven point one one percent is about two thousand six hundred ninety-one dollars a month, versus about two thousand four hundred sixty a year ago at six point two four percent.

lines.text: That's about $231 more every month, principal and interest only, by our math.
lines.say: That's about two hundred thirty-one dollars more every month, principal and interest only, by our math.

lines.text: Home equity lines, and many new car and personal loans, also tend to get pricier when rates rise.
lines.say: Home equity lines, and many new car and personal loans, also tend to get pricier when rates rise.

lines.text: Now the good news. Savers tend to come out ahead, because savings and CD rates usually follow the Fed's rate.
lines.say: Now the good news. Savers tend to come out ahead, because savings and C D rates usually follow the Fed's rate.

lines.text: Bankrate's top listed savings rate on November 7th was 4.35%. The FDIC's national average is about 0.38%.
lines.say: Bankrate's top listed savings rate on November seventh was four point three five percent. The F D I C's national average is about zero point three eight percent.

lines.text: On $10,000 for a year, that's about $38 versus about $435, by our math.
lines.say: On ten thousand dollars for a year, that's about thirty-eight dollars versus about four hundred thirty-five, by our math.

lines.text: Same Fed, very different payouts. The gap between the average and the top is where savers gain or lose.
lines.say: Same Fed, very different payouts. The gap between the average and the top is where savers gain or lose.

lines.text: Then your paycheck. In October, average hourly pay was up 3.1% from a year earlier.
lines.say: Then your paycheck. In October, average hourly pay was up three point one percent from a year earlier.

lines.text: But prices were up 3.7% in September, the last yearly number we have. So prices are still running ahead of pay.
lines.say: But prices were up three point seven percent in September, the last yearly number we have. So prices are still running ahead of pay.

lines.text: That gap is what the Fed is trying to close: slow price growth down so paychecks can catch up.
lines.say: That gap is what the Fed is trying to close: slow price growth down so paychecks can catch up.

lines.text: The risk is that higher rates also cool hiring. That's the trade-off every hiking cycle carries.
lines.say: The risk is that higher rates also cool hiring. That's the trade-off every hiking cycle carries.

lines.text: Savers and price growth can get relief, while borrowers pay more and job growth can slow.
lines.say: Savers and price growth can get relief, while borrowers pay more and job growth can slow.

lines.text: Chapter 5: What to watch next.
lines.say: Chapter five: what to watch next.

lines.text: Here's the calendar. Thursday, November 19th: Freddie Mac's next mortgage survey, to see if the streak reaches five weeks.
lines.say: Here's the calendar. Thursday, November nineteenth: Freddie Mac's next mortgage survey, to see if the streak reaches five weeks.

lines.text: Then December 8th and 9th, the Fed's meeting, with the decision on Wednesday the 9th.
lines.say: Then December eighth and ninth, the Fed's meeting, with the decision on Wednesday the ninth.

lines.text: And here's the twist: the next inflation report comes out the day after, on December 10th.
lines.say: And here's the twist: the next inflation report comes out the day after, on December tenth.

lines.text: So the Fed will decide without November's inflation number in hand.
lines.say: So the Fed will decide without November's inflation number in hand.

lines.text: That December meeting also brings the Fed's new projections, including the dot plot of where officials see rates heading.
lines.say: That December meeting also brings the Fed's new projections, including the dot plot of where officials see rates heading.

lines.text: Traders see a hike as very likely. The open question is a quarter point or a half point.
lines.say: Traders see a hike as very likely. The open question is a quarter point or a half point.

lines.text: But odds aren't promises. Data that comes in softer, or rougher, can change the mood quickly.
lines.say: But odds aren't promises. Data that comes in softer, or rougher, can change the mood quickly.

lines.text: And remember this week's lesson: mortgage rates react to expectations, so they can move before the Fed does anything.
lines.say: And remember this week's lesson: mortgage rates react to expectations, so they can move before the Fed does anything.

lines.text: Chapter 6: The recap.
lines.say: Chapter six: the recap.

lines.text: Recap. October prices rose 0.4% in a month, hotter than expected, with no yearly number because of the 2025 shutdown.
lines.say: Recap. October prices rose zero point four percent in a month, hotter than expected, with no yearly number because of the twenty twenty-five shutdown.

lines.text: A Fed governor said a half-point hike should be considered if core inflation stayed hot, and core came in at 0.3%.
lines.say: A Fed governor said a half-point hike should be considered if core inflation stayed hot, and core came in at zero point three percent.

lines.text: Mortgage rates still fell for a fourth week, to 7.11%, because they follow bond markets, not the Fed directly.
lines.say: Mortgage rates still fell for a fourth week, to seven point one one percent, because they follow bond markets, not the Fed directly.

lines.text: And the dollar hit a 19-month high, while the yen slid back near 160.
lines.say: And the dollar hit a nineteen-month high, while the yen slid back near one hundred sixty.

lines.text: For your money: card rates and savings rates move with the Fed, while fixed loans you already have don't move at all.
lines.say: For your money: card rates and savings rates move with the Fed, while fixed loans you already have don't move at all.

lines.text: So rates up, mortgages down isn't a contradiction. It's markets moving first, and now you know why.
lines.say: So rates up, mortgages down isn't a contradiction. It's markets moving first, and now you know why.

post.title: The Fed May Hike in December. So Why Did Mortgage Rates Just Fall?
post.ig: The Fed may hike in December, yet mortgage rates just fell a 4th week to 7.11%. Here's why.
post.tiktok: The Fed may hike, yet mortgage rates fell a 4th straight week to 7.11%. Here's why, and what it means for you.
post.yt_desc:
October prices rose 0.4% in a month, hotter than expected, and Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a half-point December hike should be considered if core inflation stayed hot. Yet Freddie Mac's 30-year mortgage rate fell for a fourth straight week, to 7.11%, while the dollar hit a 19-month high and the yen slid back near 160. This video explains why mortgage rates move before the Fed does, who wins and loses from a strong dollar, and what a December hike would mean for your credit card, mortgage, savings and paycheck.
